End of reading? A post-literate society in the making
2026-08-28T00:15:02+06:00 | Faridul Alam
https://www.thedailystar.net/slow-reads/wisdom/news/end-reading-post-literate-society-the-making-4257976

What happens to a culture when reading ceases to be its privileged epistemic framework—when the long passage from orality and logocentrism through graphocentrism gives way to a post-graphocentric condition in which AI no longer merely reads texts but participates in their production, transformation, and circulation?

The question points to something more consequential than a decline in book reading. It may signal a gradual movement away from the graphocentric organization of knowledge—the privileging of writing, inscription, and textuality—without a corresponding return to the logocentric valorization of speech, presence, and the immediacy of the spoken word. The trajectory, therefore, is not simply from the oral to the literate and from the literate to the post-literate. What may be emerging is a communicative configuration in which neither writing nor speech holds an uncontested epistemic center.

Rose Horowitch's “The End of Reading Is Here,” published in The Atlantic on July 8, 2026, gives this question a particularly timely urgency. Horowitch argues that the decline of sustained reading may signal the emergence of a postliterate society, extending her concern beyond declining book consumption to the weakening of habits associated with sustained reading—attention, concentration, sequential reasoning, and the willingness to remain with a text long enough for its complexity to become apparent. The displacement of books by smartphones, short-form video, and social media may consequently represent a reconfiguration of the relationship between human beings and written language.

Yet Horowitch's diagnosis leaves open a deeper question. If reading is losing its privileged cultural position, are we witnessing the displacement of literacy by a post-literate condition, or the emergence of a new interface in which literacy survives alongside other communicative schemata? The distinction matters. The first formulation suggests succession; the second signals transformation—or, better still, a paradigm shift.

Artificial intelligence complicates the matter still further. We are entering an environment in which machines can not only retrieve and reorganize existing texts but summarize, interpret, imitate, and generate language on a scale that arguably vastly exceeds individual human capacity. The paradox is striking: at the very moment when sustained human reading appears to be losing cultural centrality, textual production is becoming virtually inexhaustible.

We are entering an environment in which machines can not only retrieve and reorganize existing texts but summarize, interpret, imitate, and generate language on a scale that arguably vastly exceeds individual human capacity. The paradox is striking: at the very moment when sustained human reading appears to be losing cultural centrality, textual production is becoming virtually inexhaustible.

Artificial intelligence complicates the matter still further. We are entering an environment in which machines can not only retrieve and reorganize existing texts but summarize, interpret, imitate, and generate language on a scale that arguably vastly exceeds individual human capacity. The paradox is striking: at the very moment when sustained human reading appears to be losing cultural centrality, textual production is becoming virtually inexhaustible.

Beyond the narrative of replacement The history of communication is often narrated as a sequence of substitutions: oral culture gives way to literate culture, literate culture to print culture, and print culture to digital or post-literate culture. Such a teleological account is attractive because it turns technological history into a seemingly progressive sequence. Yet it also encourages us to imagine that each new medium supersedes the one before it, without adequately considering what is gained, what is lost, and what is reconfigured in the process.

McLuhan's insight that the medium participates in shaping perception is pertinent here. Yet the present transformation is unlikely to be understood as simple technological displacement. What changes with the emergence of a new medium is not simply which medium survives, but the relationship among communicative registers.

Jack Goody's The Interface Between the Written and the Oral offers a more productive way of thinking about this relationship. The significance of the written and the oral does not lie simply in their opposition, but in their interaction. Writing does not abolish speech, just as literacy does not eliminate oral practices. Literate societies remain profoundly oral; oral traditions can become written; written texts can return to performance.

This insight suggests that media history is better understood not as a succession of replacements but as an accumulation of interfaces. Each new communicative formation enters an already inhabited world, alters the conditions under which earlier forms operate, and is itself shaped by what it appears to supersede. The movement from orality to literacy, therefore, is not a movement from one closed cultural system into another. What emerges is a more complicated communicative ecology in which speech, writing, image, performance, print, network, and machine-generated language form an increasingly complex configuration.

The transition nevertheless involves real tensions. One useful way of approaching them is through what might be called the “winsome and losesome” of media transformation: what a new communicative form makes possible and what it renders less central. But this distinction is best understood as a heuristic rather than a balance sheet. What seems lost may later return in altered form; what emerges as gain may create dependencies not previously recognized.

One useful way of approaching them is through what might be called the “winsome and losesome” of media transformation: what a new communicative form makes possible and what it renders less central. But this distinction is best understood as a heuristic rather than a balance sheet. What seems lost may later return in altered form; what emerges as gain may create dependencies not previously recognized.

The history of communication may therefore be understood less as a linear succession than as a complex and evolving ecology. Ilya Prigogine's reflections on self-organizing systems are suggestive in this regard. New communicative forms do not simply replace earlier ones; they enter existing configurations, generate new interactions, create instabilities, and give rise to emergent forms whose properties cannot be fully predicted in advance.

Orality and the problem of presence In an oral culture, knowledge is substantially embodied in people and enacted through performance. The storyteller does not merely reproduce an immutable text. Each telling is responsive to an audience, an occasion, a place, a memory, and a particular social circumstance. Meaning resides not only in words but in voice, gesture, rhythm, intonation, and participation.

The great strength of orality is therefore presence. Its vulnerability is that the very conditions that make oral communication dynamic also make it dependent upon memory and repetition. What is transmitted can survive for generations, but it can also be altered in transmission. Variation is both a threat to exact preservation and a condition of cultural survival. From one perspective, then, orality appears to gain presence at the expense of permanence. But even that formulation is provisional. Oral traditions can be extraordinarily durable; their permanence simply takes a different form: not the permanence of inscription but the persistence of collective memory and repeated performance.

Writing changes this relationship between language and time. An utterance disappears when the speaker ceases to speak. An inscription can survive the speaker by decades, centuries, even millennia. Writing externalizes memory and turns language into something that can be revisited independently of the moment of its production. This makes possible forms of intellectual activity difficult to sustain through speech alone. A written text can be compared with another text, classified, annotated, quoted, challenged, translated, and reread. Writing does more than preserve language. It gives language a new kind of distance from itself. The reader can pause, return, reconsider, and compare. Writing thus makes possible a distinctive form of sustained and recursive attention.

Yet once again the interface complicates the binary. Writing may preserve an oral tradition. A written text may be performed. A novel may become theater. An archive may become oral history. The written and the oral remain in conversation.

Writing and its discontents In an earlier essay, “Writing and Its Discontents,” I approached writing not as a transparent container for already completed thought but as an inherently unstable and contested practice. Writing seeks to preserve meaning, yet the act of preservation removes the text from the complete control of its author. Once written, a text enters contexts the author cannot anticipate. It acquires readers the author cannot know and meanings the author cannot entirely determine.

Writing therefore contains its own discontent. The author writes in an attempt to stabilize meaning; the text, once released, becomes available for reinterpretation. The reader is not merely a recipient of the author's meaning but a participant in its interpretation and rearticulation. Reading can itself become a form of rewriting. This is where intertextuality becomes crucial. No text exists in isolation because no act of writing or reading begins from an empty linguistic space. Every text enters a field of previous texts, languages, conventions, memories, assumptions, and interpretations. Reading is consequently never simply the recovery of a meaning deposited by an author. It is an encounter among texts, contexts, and readers.

The circuit is therefore not simply writing → reading, but writing → reading → interpretation → rewriting. Rewriting need not mean producing another conventional written text. It may take the form of quotation, commentary, translation, adaptation, citation, appropriation, or reinterpretation. The written text thus survives not by remaining fixed but by entering successive contexts in which it can be contested and rearticulated. Written culture is consequently not merely a culture of preservation but a culture of accumulation, contestation, and rearticulation.

It may take the form of quotation, commentary, translation, adaptation, citation, appropriation, or reinterpretation. The written text thus survives not by remaining fixed but by entering successive contexts in which it can be contested and rearticulated. Written culture is consequently not merely a culture of preservation but a culture of accumulation, contestation, and rearticulation.

This becomes important when we turn to the contemporary digital environment. Digital media have not simply displaced writing; they have multiplied its forms and accelerated its circulation. Text now exists alongside image, sound, video, hyperlink, interface, and algorithmic generation. The reader can become commentator, distributor, remixer, or writer almost instantaneously. The digital environment compresses and reconfigures the textual circuit, while algorithmic systems participate directly in the production, transformation, and circulation of text.

The apparent retreat of reading may therefore coincide with a remarkable proliferation of textuality. What is changing is not necessarily the disappearance of the text but its place within the communicative order. Literacy may be losing its privileged cultural position without becoming obsolete.

Post-literacy is not post-textuality The post-literate society is not a society without writing. On the contrary, it may be a society of too much writing. Post-literacy is not the disappearance of writing but the decentering of literacy amid a remarkable proliferation of textuality. Messages, captions, comments, articles, transcripts, subtitles, posts, reviews, summaries, and generated texts now circulate at a velocity and volume unimaginable within the traditional print economy. Artificial intelligence accelerates this proliferation by making the generation of language increasingly inexpensive and immediate.

The scarcity no longer pertains to text; it increasingly applies to attention. This shift transforms the cultural economy of reading. When texts were relatively scarce and difficult to reproduce, the reader's primary problem was often access. In the digital environment, abundance shifts the problem from access to discernment—what deserves engagement, what may be delegated or ignored, and how we distinguish reliable interpretation from algorithmically produced assertion. What deserves to be read? What can be ignored or summarized? Which interpretation should be trusted? Which recommendations reflect our own judgment, and which have been algorithmically produced?

Literacy therefore becomes more than the ability to read and write. It increasingly involves the ability to select, evaluate, interpret, and navigate an overwhelming field of textual and multimodal information. The post-literate condition looks less like the disappearance of literacy than its transformation: writing proliferates even as reading becomes more selective, mediated, and contested.

The return of orality through the interface Digital media do not simply replace literacy with orality. They selectively reactivate features long associated with oral communication—immediacy, dialogue, performance, responsiveness, and the presence of voice and image—but reconstitute them within technological conditions fundamentally different from those of primary orality. A podcast may be conversational and intimate yet remains recorded, edited, distributed, and reproducible; a livestream creates immediacy and audience interaction yet can be archived, replayed, clipped, and recirculated; a social-media post is written but may function rhetorically like speech—rapid, dialogic, responsive, and seemingly ephemeral—even as it remains searchable, copyable, and algorithmically retrievable.

What returns, therefore, is not primary orality but something closer to technologically mediated orality: oral forms of interaction reconstituted within infrastructures of writing, recording, storage, and computation. The storyteller becomes a streamer; the audience becomes a networked public; memory becomes both archive and database; performance becomes recorded and quantifiable; conversation becomes searchable and reproducible. What was once ephemeral can now persist indefinitely, while what appears immediate may already be technologically mediated and archived.

The post-literate environment therefore does not take us backward into an oral society. Rather, it reconfigures orality, literacy, and visuality within a shared technological infrastructure, where modalities increasingly overlap and become convertible: text becomes voice, voice becomes text, speech becomes transcript, image becomes caption, conversation becomes data, data becomes generated language. These conversions, however, are never neutral. Each changes what is preserved and what is lost, what becomes visible and what becomes retrievable. Speech converted into text gains durability and searchability but may lose gesture, tone, timing, and other dimensions of embodied presence. The contemporary subject consequently moves among modalities without necessarily experiencing them as discrete media.

From intertextuality to intermediality This is where intertextuality begins to shade into intermediality. No text exists alone, but increasingly no medium exists alone either. A text can become a podcast; a podcast can become a transcript; the transcript can become a summary; the summary can become a prompt; the prompt can generate another text. An image can be described in language, language can produce an image, and both can be incorporated into another communicative artifact.

The boundaries among media become increasingly porous. The consequence is paradoxical. We may be becoming more intertextual while becoming less deeply engaged with individual texts. The relations among texts multiply even as the time available for sustained textual encounter contracts. If post-literacy means the disappearance of writing, it is misleading. If it means the declining cultural centrality of sustained reading within an environment saturated by other modes of communication, it becomes considerably more useful.

Homo grammatologicus This is where the concept of Homo grammatologicus becomes relevant. The traditional writing subject assumed a fundamental distinction between the human writer and the written artifact: writing was a human technology for externalizing thought. AI unsettles that distinction by introducing the machine as a participant in the production, transformation, and circulation of linguistic forms. Code writes. Algorithms write. Generative systems write. Humans write with machines.

The result is not necessarily the disappearance of the human author but the destabilization of the boundaries through which authorship has traditionally been understood. Who writes when a human formulates an instruction, a machine generates a passage, a human revises it, and an algorithm determines who encounters it? The question is therefore not merely one of authorship or ownership. It is a question about the provenance of language. Writing, which once externalized human memory, is becoming a process in which human and machine production can be increasingly difficult to disentangle.

Yet even here, the logic of simple replacement fails. AI may displace some forms of reading by providing summaries in place of sustained engagement with books, but it may also introduce readers to texts they might otherwise never encounter. It can generate formulaic prose, but it can also enable inexperienced writers to experiment with forms beyond their previous technical competence. It can substitute for interpretation, yet it can also expose readers to competing interpretations and provoke further inquiry. The same technology can diminish one capacity while extending another, displace one form of intellectual labor while making another possible.

What matters, then, is not simply what AI replaces, but what relations among writing, reading, interpretation, authorship, and mediation it reconfigures. In this sense, Homo grammatologicus names not the end of the human writer but the emergence of a writing subject whose linguistic production increasingly occurs at the interface between human intention and machine mediation.

The limits of the winsome and losesome This is precisely where the winsome/losesome paradigm reaches its limit. Cultural change is rarely a simple exchange in which one capacity disappears as another emerges. What is displaced in one context may be revitalized in another; a new capacity may create a new dependency; a new convenience may introduce a new vulnerability. The more appropriate concept, therefore, is reconfiguration.

Orality persists within literacy. Literacy persists within digitality. Digitality reorganizes both. AI increasingly mediates the relations among all three. The communicative order is consequently becoming layered rather than sequential. Each new formation enters an existing ecology, altering the conditions under which earlier forms continue to operate. The winsome/losesome distinction nevertheless remains valuable as a heuristic. Its simplification can make a transformation initially intelligible. But a paradigm is an instrument of inquiry, not an immutable description of reality.

Reading and the problem of intellectual friction This is why the concern about post-literacy should not be reduced to the proposition that people are reading fewer books. The more consequential issue may be the changing status of sustained attention—and, with it, the forms of memory, interpretation, and intellectual agency that sustained attention makes possible.

Deep reading asks the reader to remain with difficulty, ambiguity, sequence, and delayed resolution. It requires a willingness not merely to extract information from a text but to inhabit it long enough for meanings to unfold, conflict, and perhaps remain unresolved. The contemporary media environment, by contrast, frequently encourages a different epistemic disposition: Tell me what it means. Summarize it. Give me the answer. Make it shorter. There is nothing inherently wrong with these practices. Concision, accessibility, searchability, and rapid synthesis can enlarge rather than diminish intellectual possibility. The difficulty begins when convenience ceases to be merely a useful feature of a medium and becomes an epistemological principle—when the distinction between knowing what a text says and understanding how its meaning is produced begins to disappear.

At stake, then, is not simply the quantity of reading but the relationship between attention and understanding. When interpretation can always be outsourced, interpretation itself may become less visible as a form of intellectual labor. When difficulty can always be removed, difficulty may begin to appear unnecessary rather than constitutive of understanding. When answers are continually supplied before questions have had time to mature, the capacity to dwell in uncertainty may itself become culturally attenuated. One genuine risk associated with post-literacy, therefore, may be not ignorance but the erosion of intellectual friction: the gradual weakening of habits that make sustained inquiry possible.

When interpretation can always be outsourced, interpretation itself may become less visible as a form of intellectual labor. When difficulty can always be removed, difficulty may begin to appear unnecessary rather than constitutive of understanding. When answers are continually supplied before questions have had time to mature, the capacity to dwell in uncertainty may itself become culturally attenuated. One genuine risk associated with post-literacy, therefore, may be not ignorance but the erosion of intellectual friction: the gradual weakening of habits that make sustained inquiry possible.

Yet even this claim requires qualification. It would be a mistake to turn the defense of deep reading into nostalgia for print. Digital archives can enable forms of comparative research and retrieval unimaginable within a purely print environment. Hypertext can foster associative and non-linear forms of reading. Audiobooks can sustain extended encounters with complex works through modalities other than visual reading. Even AI can function not merely as a substitute for interpretation but as an intellectual interlocutor that prompts questions, exposes assumptions, generates alternatives, and sends the reader back to the text with a more differentiated set of inquiries.

The issue, therefore, is neither whether the new medium is good or bad nor whether literacy is being simply displaced by post-literacy. The more significant question is what configurations of attention, memory, interpretation, and agency different media cultivate, constrain, or make possible. A post-literate culture may not be one in which reading disappears, but one in which reading becomes one practice among several within a more heterogeneous ecology of meaning-making. The challenge is to ensure that the expansion of available modes does not come at the cost of our capacity to remain with what cannot be immediately summarized, answered, or resolved.

Knowledge at the interface There is a larger epistemological implication. Knowledge has never been produced independently of the communicative forms through which it circulates. The medium does not mechanically determine knowledge, but neither is knowledge indifferent to the conditions of its inscription, preservation, retrieval, and interpretation. Each configuration—oral, written, digital, AI-mediated—makes certain forms of knowledge easier to produce and others more difficult to sustain. But none should be regarded as epistemically final.

Indeed, the post-literate environment may make the contestability of knowledge more visible than ever. When an answer can be generated instantly, the question of how that answer was formulated becomes more important, not less. When multiple interpretations can be produced simultaneously, the distinction between information and understanding becomes more difficult but also more consequential. The challenge is therefore not to recover some supposedly uncontaminated form of knowledge. It is to develop the critical capacity to move among competing forms of mediation without mistaking accessibility for certainty.

Toward a post-literate interface Artificial intelligence intensifies the ambiguity. It does not merely threaten reading; it unsettles the inherited relationships among writing, reading, interpretation, memory, and mediation. It can summarize a book and discourage reading it—or provide an entry point that makes the book newly approachable. It can generate prose and encourage passivity—or become an interlocutor through which a writer discovers how to revise, question, and rethink. It can flatten complexity, but it can also make complexity accessible to readers who might otherwise be excluded from it.

The consequences, therefore, cannot be determined by the technology alone. They will depend upon how technological capacities are incorporated into cultural practices, educational institutions, and habits of attention. The same tool can diminish intellectual agency in one context and enlarge it in another. What matters is not simply what AI can do, but what humans learn to expect from it—and what they cease to do for themselves when those expectations become habitual.

This brings us back to Goody. The future is unlikely to be purely oral, purely literate, or simply post-literate. It is more likely to be an interface: a dynamic and unstable configuration in which speech, writing, image, performance, print, archive, network, algorithm, and machine-generated language coexist, overlap, and continually modify one another. The result may be neither the triumph nor the demise of literacy, but the emergence of a communicative ecology whose properties cannot yet be fully specified.

What changes at this interface, perhaps most profoundly, is the old relationship between presence and absence. Orality once appeared to privilege presence, while writing preserved language across the speaker's absence. Digital and AI-mediated communication increasingly unsettle that distinction, producing forms of presence that are simultaneously recordable, reproducible, searchable, and no longer dependent on physical co-presence

The post-literate question, therefore, is not simply: What will replace reading? It is: What new configuration of reading, writing, speaking, seeing, remembering, and machine-mediated interpretation is coming into being? We do not yet know. But that uncertainty is not a weakness in the argument; it is intrinsic to the transition itself. New media rarely produce the future in the form initially imagined for them. They enter existing cultures, encounter inherited practices, acquire unforeseen uses, create new dependencies, revive older capacities in altered forms, and generate consequences that exceed their original intentions.

The future of reading, then, may not be a choice between survival and disappearance. It may be transformation at the interface—where the oral, the written, the visual, the digital, and the computational increasingly meet, contest, supplement, and remake one another. Perhaps, then, the post-literate society is not the society after literacy. It is the society in which literacy is no longer alone. And this may be the more consequential transformation: not the disappearance of reading or writing, but the emergence of a communicative world in which no single medium can any longer claim an uncontested monopoly over how culture remembers, interprets, and produces knowledge. The question is not which medium will prevail, but what kind of culture emerges when their boundaries become increasingly permeable—and when human attention, judgment, and agency must navigate an ecology in which meaning is no longer produced, preserved, or interpreted by any single mode of communication.

Dr. Faridul Alam, a former academic, writes from New York City.
